bullets: Many British soldiers were **working-class volunteers** who enlisted because of unemployment and poverty: exactly the situation stanza 4 describes.
The Boer War was controversial: British concentration camps and heavy losses led to criticism at home. Hardy was sceptical about war and **questioned patriotic propaganda**.
Hardy often wrote about ordinary rural people and their dialect, and about the cruel indifference of fate.
Compare with Tennyson (1854): only fifty years apart, but Hardy’s soldier questions where Tennyson’s soldiers do not ‘reason why’.

callouts.p: Writing during the Boer War, when many soldiers enlisted to escape unemployment, Hardy gives a voice to an ordinary volunteer to show that the ‘enemy’ was just as ordinary.

core.h: Context (AO3): Hardy and the Boer War
core.p: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) was a novelist and poet from Dorset (his fictional ‘Wessex’). He wrote The Man He Killed in **1902**, during the **Second Boer War (1899–1902)** in South Africa, in which Britain fought Dutch-descended Boer settlers.

bullets: **Conflict type**: military conflict seen through one personal act; inner conflict of conscience.
**Big message**: enemies share a common humanity; war forces ordinary men to kill for no personal reason.
**Perspective**: first-person dramatic monologue; the title’s third person (‘He’) makes the speaker anonymous and representative.
core.p: A soldier explains that if he had met the man he killed in a pub, they would have shared drinks. Instead, as soldiers facing each other, they fired and he killed him. He tries to say why (‘because he was my foe’) but falters, imagines that the other man enlisted for the same reasons he did (unemployment, no other reason), and concludes that war is ‘quaint and curious’: you kill a man you would otherwise have treated or lent money to.

bullets: The regular rhyme contrasts with the **broken syntax** of stanzas 3–4: the form tries to stay orderly while his thinking falls apart.
**Enjambment across the stanza break** (stanza 3 into 4: ‘although’) is the only one in the poem; it shows doubt overflowing.
**Cyclical structure**: starts and ends with the pub image, peace framing war.
The **title**’s third person (‘He’) creates distance; the poem’s first person removes it.
core.p: Five **quatrains** with an **ABAB** rhyme scheme and a ballad-like metre (lines 1, 2 and 4 are short; line 3 is longer). The regular, simple form is like a folk song or a conversation in a pub.

bullets: War is **senseless and arbitrary**: the soldier cannot give a real reason.
Enemies are **alike**: parallel syntax and ‘just as I’.
War is caused by **economic circumstances**, not hatred.
**Psychological aftermath**: the speaker is still talking it through, unresolved.
**Understatement** (‘quaint and curious’) reveals trauma he cannot express directly.

callouts.p: An ordinary soldier tries and fails to justify killing a man just like himself.

essays.q: Compare how soldiers’ thoughts about killing are presented in The Man He Killed and The Charge of the Light Brigade.
essays.text: Tennyson presents soldiers who do not think about killing at all. The anaphora of ‘Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why’ sounds like a military code, and the confident dactylic rhythm carries the men forward as a single body, ‘the six hundred’. Hardy deliberately gives his soldier what Tennyson’s soldiers lack: a voice and a reason to question. When he tries to explain, ‘I shot him dead because —’, the dash breaks the line at the exact moment the reason should arrive, and the repetition of ‘because’ in the next line shows him searching. His over-insistent ‘Just so’ and ‘of course’ suggest he is trying to convince himself. While Tennyson’s regular structure reflects a Victorian confidence in duty, Hardy’s regular quatrains are disrupted by dashes and the poem’s only enjambed stanza break, so the form itself seems to falter. Writing during the Boer War, when many volunteers enlisted to escape unemployment, Hardy has his speaker realise that the dead man joined up ‘just as I’, a recognition that Tennyson’s poem, built to make the nation ‘Honour’ its soldiers, never allows.
essays.thesis: Tennyson celebrates soldiers who do not question their orders, while Hardy, writing half a century later, gives a soldier the voice to question and shows that he cannot find an answer.
why: Clear conceptual contrast (not reasoning vs reasoning and failing).
AO2 on anaphora, dashes, rhythm and stanza structure.
AO3 contrasting Victorian duty with Boer War recruitment.

It was written in 1902 about the Boer War; it predates WW1.

poem.how: The whole poem is in speech marks: imagine a working man talking to a friend in a pub.

stanzas.label: Stanza 1: what might have been
lines: We should have sat us down to wet

notes.n: Opens with a **conditional** (‘Had…’): an imagined alternative world of peace. ‘He and I’ pairs the two men as equals from the first line.
**Tautology** (old and ancient mean the same): sounds like ordinary, unpolished speech. The pub is a symbol of community and friendship.
**Colloquial** idiom for drinking: the speaker is a working-class man, not a poet.
A small measure of ale: **dialect** word (Hardy’s Wessex). The exclamation mark makes the friendship sound warm and real.
The **opening speech marks** show this is a **dramatic monologue**: Hardy gives the voice to an ordinary soldier, not an officer or a poet.

stanzas.label: Stanza 2: the killing
lines: I shot at him as he at me,
And killed him in his place.

notes.n: ‘But’ is the turn from imagined peace to the reality of war. ‘Ranged’ suggests they were placed in rows by others: they did not choose to fight.
Close, personal combat: each sees the other as a person. Makes the killing more disturbing.
**Parallel syntax** shows the two men are identical: the only difference is who shot first. Mutual, equal violence.
notes.w: I shot at him as he at me,

notes.n: Blunt, **monosyllabic** statement. ‘In his place’ can mean on the spot, but also hints that the speaker could have been in his place: it could have been the other way round.
notes.w: And killed him in his place.

stanzas.label: Stanza 3: the struggle to justify
lines: Just so: my foe of course he was;

notes.n: The **dash** creates a hesitation: he cannot find a reason. The pause at the end of the line is the moment his certainty breaks.
**Repetition** of ‘because’ shows him groping for an explanation. ‘Foe’ is an official, old-fashioned word, as if borrowed from propaganda.
Over-insistent phrases (‘Just so’, ‘of course’) suggest he is **trying to convince himself**. Inner conflict.
notes.w: Just so: my foe of course he was;

notes.n: ‘Although’ undercuts his certainty and is **enjambed** across the stanza break: his doubt literally spills over the structure.

stanzas.label: Stanza 4: seeing himself in the enemy
lines: Was out of work — had sold his traps —

notes.n: ‘List’ = enlist. The speaker imagines his victim’s life and realises they are alike. ‘Perhaps’ shows he is speculating, but with sympathy.
**Dashes** fragment the line, mimicking hesitant speech. ‘Just as I’ makes the identification explicit: the enemy is a mirror.
Economic reasons for enlisting: unemployment and poverty (‘traps’ = belongings or tools). Links to **Boer War recruitment** of the working poor.
notes.w: Was out of work — had sold his traps —

notes.n: Bleak conclusion: men killed each other for no personal reason at all.

stanzas.label: Stanza 5: ‘quaint and curious’
lines: You'd treat if met where any bar is,

notes.n: **Understatement and irony**: ‘quaint and curious’ are mild words for killing, as if he cannot face the horror. The **inverted syntax** (‘war is!’) sounds awkward, like someone forcing out a conclusion.
notes.w: Yes; quaint and curious war is!

notes.n: Switch to the generalising **second person** ‘you’: his experience becomes everyone’s. ‘Fellow’ is friendly, shocking beside ‘shoot’.
Returns to the pub image of stanza 1: **cyclical structure**. Peace and war are separated only by circumstance.
notes.w: You'd treat if met where any bar is,

notes.n: Half a crown (2s 6d) is a small loan: ordinary kindness he would have shown. Ends on everyday decency, highlighting the absurdity of war.

summary: The Man He Killed (1902) is Thomas Hardy’s dramatic monologue in which an ordinary soldier struggles to explain why he shot a man who, in peacetime, might have been his drinking friend; compare how it presents the senselessness of war, the shared humanity of enemies and inner conflict, with context of the Boer War.

terms.d: A poem spoken by a character (not the poet) to a listener.
Presenting something as less serious than it is (‘quaint and curious’).
Repeating a grammatical structure to show equality or contrast.
Ending where the poem began (the pub).
A pause in the middle of a line, often marked by punctuation.
